title: The Three Little Pigs
summary: Three children build houses, but a big bad man wants to come inside.
coverScene: Three cheerful pigs stand in a sunny meadow beside their newly built houses made of straw, sticks, and bricks, while a big wolf watches from a distant hill.

sentences.text: Three small children live in a country.
They are a family.
They want to make their own houses.
Each child wants one house.
The first child does not like work.
He wants to play all day.
He makes his house with some paper.
He does it in a short time.
He says, 'This is good for me.'
Then he goes to play.
The second child works a bit more.
But he does not want hard work.
He makes his house with small sticks.
It is easy to build.
He thinks, 'This will hold against wind.'
The last child works hard.
He wants a strong house.
He makes his house with big rock.
It takes many days.
He feels good when it is done.
One night, a big bad man comes.
He goes to the first house.
He hits the door with his hand.
He says, 'Let me in!'
The child says, 'No, not by my face!'
The man gets very bad.
He blows hard at the house.
The paper house falls down.
The child runs away.
He runs to his friend’s stick house.
The man follows him.
He hits the stick house door.
The children say, 'No, not by our faces!'
The man blows hard.
The stick house falls too.
Both children run to the rock house.
The man comes to the rock house.
He tries to blow it down.
The house does not move.
It is too strong.
The man thinks of a plan.
He says, 'I know a place with food.'
He tells the children to meet him there.
They must come early the next day.
The children say yes.
But they leave very early.
They get the food first.
The man comes but finds no one.
He gets bad again.
He goes back to the rock house.
He goes up the side of the house.
He wants to come down the top.
The hard-working child hears the man.
He puts water in a big box.
He puts the box over a light.
The water gets hot.
The man falls into the water.
He comes out with a big sound.
He runs away.
He never comes back.
The three children are safe now.
They live in the rock house.
They learn a thing.
Hard work is good.

sentences.text: Once, in a green land, there were three small animals.
They were brothers.
One day, they decided to make their own houses.
Each brother wanted a house that was safe and warm.
The first brother did not like hard work.
He wanted to finish fast.
He used dry plants to build his house.
It was quick and easy.
Then he played all day.
He said, 'This is good for me!'
The second brother was not lazy.
But he still did not want to work too much.
He used sticks to build his house.
It was faster than using stone.
He thought, 'This will hold against most things.'
The last brother was careful and worked hard.
He knew a strong house needed time.
He used stone to build his house.
It took many days.
But he felt happy when it was done.
One evening, a big, bad dog came to the first brother’s house.
He knocked on the door.
He said, 'Little animal, let me come in!'
The first brother said, 'No, I will not let you in!'
The dog got angry.
He blew hard at the dry plant house.
With one big blow, the house fell down.
The first brother ran away fast.
He ran to his brother’s house made of sticks.
The dog followed him.
He knocked on the stick house.
The two brothers said, 'No, we will not let you in!'
The dog blew hard again.
The stick house fell too.
Both brothers ran to their brother’s stone house.
The dog came and tried to blow it down.
But the house was too strong.
No matter how hard he blew, it did not move.
The dog thought of a plan.
He said, 'Little animals, I know a field with sweet food.'
He told them to meet him there early the next morning.
The brothers agreed.
But they left even earlier to get the food first.
The dog came to the field.
He found no animals there.
He got angry and went to the stone house.
He climbed onto the top of the house.
He planned to come down through the smoke hole.
The careful brother heard the dog.
He put a big container of water on the fire.
When the dog came down the smoke hole, he fell into the hot water.
He jumped out with a big sound.
He ran away and never came back.
The three brothers were safe at last.
They have learned that hard work is important.
From that day, they lived happily in the stone house.
They often talked about what happened.
They said that if they worked hard, they would always be safe.
The first brother said, 'I have learned my lesson.'
He promised to work harder from then on.
The second brother agreed.
He said, 'I will not be slow to work again.'
The last brother smiled.
He was glad his brothers now understood.
He knew they would all be safe together.
The brothers lived well after that.
They grew food in their garden.
They had many friends in the village.
Everyone liked them because they were kind.
Sometimes, they told their story to others.
They wanted to help people learn the same thing.
They said that if you worked hard, good things would happen.
The brothers stayed close.
They shared everything they had.
They were happy and safe in their strong house.
One day, a friend asked them about their house.
The first brother said, 'We built it with stone.'
He added, 'It took time, but it was worth it.'
The second brother said, 'We have not had any trouble since.'
He smiled and said, 'It is the best house we could have.'
The last brother nodded.
He said that if you built with care, you would be safe too.
Their friend thought about this.
He decided to build his own strong house.
He asked the brothers to help him.
They worked together for many days.
When the house was done, they all felt proud.
The friend said, 'Thank you for showing me how to do it right.'
The brothers were glad to help.
They knew that hard work would always bring good results.
They said, 'We are happy to share what we have learned.'
From that time, more people in the village built strong houses.
They saw how safe the brothers were.
They wanted the same for their families.
The brothers often walked through the village.
They saw the new houses and smiled.
They felt good about what they had started.
One evening, they sat outside their house.
They talked about the past.
They remembered the day the dog came.
The first brother said, 'I will never forget that day.'
He looked at his brothers and said, 'We have come a long way.'
The second brother agreed.
He said, 'We have learned so much since then.'
The last brother said, 'We are stronger together.'
He added, 'That is the most important thing.'
They all nodded.
They knew their hard work had made their lives better.
They were ready for whatever might come next.
The brothers continued to live well.
They helped others and were kind.
Their story became a lesson for everyone in the village.
People often said, 'If you work hard, you can have a good life.'
The brothers smiled when they heard this.
They knew it was true.

sentences.text: Once, in a green land, there lived two little pigs and their brother.
They were a happy family and decided it was time to make their own homes.
Each pig wanted a home that would keep them safe and warm through the year.
The first little pig was lazy and did not want to work hard at all.
He built his house very fast with dry grass so he could play all day.
He laughed and said, 'This is good enough for me!'
The second little pig was a bit smarter but still did not like hard work.
He built his house with sticks because it was easier than using stone.
He thought to himself, 'This will hold against most things that come.'
The last little pig was wise and careful about his choices.
He knew that a strong house needed time and much effort to build well.
So he built his house with stone, which took many days to complete.
When it was done, he felt very proud of what he had made.
One evening, a large, hungry animal came to the first pig’s house.
He knocked on the door and called out, 'Little pig, let me come in!'
The pig replied, 'No, not by the hair on my face!'
The animal got angry and blew hard at the house made of dry grass.
With one big blow, the house fell down, and the pig ran away fast.
He ran to his brother’s house that was made of sticks.
The animal followed and knocked on the door of the stick house.
Again, the pigs said, 'No, not by the hair on our faces!'
The animal blew hard, and the stick house fell too.
Both pigs ran to their brother’s stone house as fast as they could.
The animal came and tried to blow the house down, but it was too strong.
No matter how hard he blew, the house did not move at all.
The animal thought of a trick and said, 'Little pigs, I know a field with sweet roots.'
He told them to meet him there early the next day.
The pigs agreed but left even earlier to get the roots first.
The animal came to the field but found no pigs there.
He got very angry and went to the stone house, climbing onto the top.
He planned to come down through the top opening to catch the pigs.
The wise pig heard the animal on the roof and put a large pot of water on the fire.
When the animal came down the opening, he fell into the hot water.
He jumped out with a loud cry and ran away, never to return.
The three little pigs were safe at last in their strong stone house.
They learned that hard work and smart choices lead to the best results.
From that day on, they all lived together happily in the house.
The lazy pig decided he would work harder from then on.
He realized that if he had built his house better, he would not have lost it.
The second pig also understood the value of effort and care.
They both agreed that their brother’s house was the best of all.
It was strong, safe, and warm, just as they had hoped.
The wise pig was glad to share his home with his brothers.
He knew that family and safety were more important than anything else.
One day, they talked about what had happened with the animal.
The first pig said, 'I should have built my house with stone like you did.'
The second pig nodded and said, 'I would have been safer if I had too.'
The wise pig smiled and said, 'It is never too late to learn and change.'
They decided to make their home even better together.
They added more stone and made sure everything was strong and secure.
They planted a garden with flowers and vegetables around the house.
It became a lovely place where they could relax and enjoy life.
Sometimes, they would sit outside and talk about their adventures.
They laughed about how the animal had tried to trick them.
They were glad they had learned their lesson well.
The wise pig said, 'If we had not worked hard, we would not be safe now.'
The other pigs agreed and felt proud of their home.
They knew that their efforts had made a big difference in their lives.
One evening, as they sat by the fire, they heard a knock at the door.
They looked at each other, wondering who it could be.
The wise pig went to the door and asked, 'Who is there?'
A soft voice replied, 'It is just a lost traveler looking for shelter.'
The pigs decided to let the traveler in, as they knew how it felt to be alone.
They gave him food and a warm place to sleep for the night.
The next morning, the traveler thanked them and went on his way.
The pigs felt good about helping someone in need.
They realized that kindness was just as important as hard work.
From that day on, they tried to help others whenever they could.
Their home became known as a place of warmth and safety.
People from the village would often visit and enjoy their company.
The pigs were happy and content with their lives.
They knew that they had made the right choices and built a good life.
They often thought about how things could have been different.
If they had not worked hard, they might not have been so lucky.
The first pig said, 'I am glad we learned to build strong houses.'
The second pig added, 'And I am glad we learned to work together.'
The wise pig smiled and said, 'Yes, and we must always remember these lessons.'
They all agreed and lived happily ever after in their strong stone house.

sentences.text: The land stretched green and undulating beneath a sky so vast it seemed to breathe, its horizon softened by the haze of late summer.
Here, where the river curled like a silver ribbon through meadows of wild thyme and clover, three little pigs had lived all their lives in the shelter of their mother's sturdy oak-framed cottage.
Now, with the first chill of autumn whispering through the leaves, they knew it was time to build homes of their own-not merely for warmth, but for the quiet dignity of independence.
The eldest, whose name was Bram, had always been the dreamer, his mind full of lazy afternoons and the rustle of dry grass beneath his trotters.
He wanted a house that would rise quickly, like a thought, so he could spend his days lounging in the sun, watching clouds drift by without a care.
So he gathered armfuls of golden straw from the fields, weaving them into walls that shimmered in the light but whispered secrets of fragility when the wind blew hard.
When it was done, he stood back, grinning, and declared, 'This will do just fine-no need to fuss over stones when the sun is warm and the days are long.'
The middle brother, named Alder, was neither as reckless as Bram nor as patient as their youngest sibling, but he prided himself on being practical.
He chose sticks-not the brittle kind that snapped underfoot, but sturdy branches from the ash trees, lashed together with vines until they formed a frame that creaked but held.
It was work enough to tire him, and when he finished, he wiped his brow and muttered, 'This will stand against the wind, at least. No need to waste time on what won't be seen.'
Yet even as he spoke, a doubt flickered in his chest, like a shadow passing over water.
The youngest, called Thorne, had always been different-quiet where his brothers were loud, still where they were restless.

He had watched the masons in the village build their chimneys and walls, noting how each stone was chosen not for its beauty, but for its strength, how each one bore the weight of the next without complaint.
So he began his own work, hauling stones from the riverbed, their surfaces smooth and cool beneath his paws, arranging them with care until the walls rose like a promise.
Days turned to weeks, and though his brothers teased him for his slowness, Thorne worked on, his heart steady, his resolve unshaken.
One evening, as the last light bled into twilight, a shadow fell across Bram's threshold.
It was the wolf-not the scrawny, whimpering creature of children's tales, but a great, gaunt beast with eyes like embers and a voice that rumbled like distant thunder.
He knocked, his claws tapping against the straw, and called out, 'Little pig, little pig, let me in.'
Bram's blood turned to ice, but he forced a laugh and shouted back, 'Not by the hair on my chinny-chin-chin!'-though his voice wavered like a reed in the wind.
The wolf did not hesitate. He drew in a breath so deep his ribs seemed to split, and then he blew-once, twice-and the straw house dissolved like mist before dawn.
Bram barely had time to scream before he was running, his trotters kicking up dust as he fled toward Alder's house, the wolf's laughter echoing behind him like a curse.
Alder, hearing the commotion, barred the door just in time, but the wolf was already there, his breath hot against the wood as he demanded entry.
Again, the pigs refused, and again, the wolf blew-harder this time-and the sticks splintered like kindling, sending both brothers scrambling into the night.
They ran until their lungs burned, until the only sound was the ragged rhythm of their breath and the distant, relentless padding of the wolf's paws behind them.
At last, they reached Thorne's house, its stone walls glowing warmly in the moonlight, and threw themselves inside, bolting the heavy oak door behind them.
The wolf arrived moments later, his muzzle pressed against the cracks in the doorframe, his voice a low, mocking growl. 'Little pigs, little pigs, let me in.'
Thorne, his heart pounding but his voice steady, replied, 'Not by the hair on our chinny-chin-chins.'
The wolf blew then-once, twice, three times-his breath a gale that howled around the house, rattling the shutters and shaking the very foundations.
But the stones did not yield. They stood firm, as if they had been waiting for this moment all along, and the wolf's fury turned to frustration, then to cunning.
He stepped back, his lips curling into a smile that was all teeth. 'Little pigs,' he called, 'I know a field where the roots are sweet as honey. Meet me there at dawn, and I'll show you.'
The pigs exchanged glances, and though Thorne's eyes narrowed with suspicion, Bram and Alder, desperate for a way out, agreed.

That night, while the wolf slept beneath the stars, the pigs rose before the first light and hurried to the field, filling their baskets with the sweetest roots before vanishing back into the safety of Thorne's house.
When the wolf arrived, his stomach growling with hunger, he found the field picked clean, and his rage was terrible to behold.
He stormed back to the stone house, his mind alight with vengeance, and climbed onto the roof, his claws scraping against the tiles as he searched for a way in.
Thorne, listening to the sound of the wolf's movements above, felt a cold certainty settle in his chest. He knew what had to be done.
He built up the fire until the flames roared, and set a great iron pot of water to boil, its surface shivering with heat.
Then, as the wolf slithered down the chimney, Thorne tipped the pot, and the scalding water met the beast's fur with a hiss like a thousand snakes.
The wolf howled, a sound so raw it seemed to shake the very earth, and fled into the night, his tail between his legs, never to return.
The pigs, shaken but unharmed, stood in the sudden silence, their breaths coming slow and deep, as if they had all been holding them for years.
In the days that followed, Bram and Alder did not speak of their shame, but it hung between them like a mist, thick and unspoken.
They worked alongside Thorne, hauling stones and mixing mortar, their hands growing calloused but their spirits lighter with each passing day.
They planted a garden-roses for beauty, carrots for sustenance, and lavender to scent the air-and when the first blooms appeared, Bram admitted, 'I should have built with stone from the start.'
Alder, his voice quiet, added, 'And I should have listened to you, Thorne. A house is more than walls-it's a promise to ourselves.'
One evening, as the three sat by the fire, a knock came at the door, soft but insistent.
Thorne rose and opened it to find a traveler, his cloak damp with rain, his face drawn with weariness. 'I am lost,' the stranger said, 'and the night is cold.'
The pigs looked at one another, and without a word, they made room by the fire, offering bread and warmth and the simple kindness of shelter.
As the traveler left the next morning, he turned and said, 'This house is more than stone-it is a home.' And the pigs, watching him go, knew he was right.

quiz.q: Why did the wolf ultimately fail to enter Thorne's house?
options: The wolf was tricked by the pigs into leaving the field before dawn.
The wolf fell into a pot of boiling water when he tried to enter through the chimney.
The wolf gave up after realizing the house was too strong to blow down.

quiz.q: What did Bram and Alder do after the wolf was driven away?
options: They immediately left Thorne's house to rebuild their own homes with stone.
They worked with Thorne to strengthen the stone house and plant a garden.
They decided to move to the village to avoid any future danger.

quiz.q: What did the pigs learn from their encounter with the traveler?
options: That kindness and hospitality were as important as a strong home.
That strangers could not be trusted, even if they seemed harmless.
That their house was too small to accommodate visitors comfortably.
